Historical appendix: Scriptural Date and Location
The date of a narrated event, the composition of a book, and a traditional attribution are different claims.
The following orientation preserves those distinctions. A book-wide span does not date each verse separately.
An unresolved occasion is left unresolved; the prayers of the Mass are not assigned biblical dates merely
because they echo biblical language. The rows reproduce the reviewed chronology, with fuller source
qualifications immediately below. They are an orientation to the sources used here, not a survey of every

Esther: a threatened people in the Persian court
The Introit takes its principal words from Mardochai’s prayer, not from a speech of the Persian king. Esther
13:8 identifies the speaker; verses 15–18 identify the threatened people and their appeal to the God who
redeemed them from Egypt. Susa belongs to the narrative setting of the court (Esth. 1:2;2:5). It is not an
established writing desk for the final book. The historical Catholic Encyclopedia article “Esther” places its
conjectural early composition near the end of Xerxes’ reign or in the reign of Artaxerxes, while explicitly
allowing later composition from older materials. The table’s compact span is therefore not a secure date of
Mardochai’s prayer, and still less a secure date of the chant’s selection. Nor does a hypothesis about the
whole book independently date the Greek prayer material preserved in the Vulgate additions.39

Twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost                                      Historical appendix: Scriptural Date and Location

Job: the land of the story and the date of the book
Hus is the Douay–Rheims form of Uz. Job 1:1 names it but supplies no chronological synchronism. The
reviewed USCCB introduction describes a probable range for the book’s composition spanning the seventh
through fifth centuries before Christ. That is a literary dating judgment, not a date of Job’s losses, nor a
settled identification of the place where the author worked. The Offertory compresses Job 1–2: it joins the
initial portrait, permitted loss of possessions and children, and the second, bodily trial. Its order must not
be flattened into a single uninterrupted quotation or treated as evidence that the first permission already
included the body.40

The Psalms: remembered events and undated prayers
Psalm 89 bears a Mosaic heading in the biblical witness; Augustine explicitly cautions that this need not
mean Moses wrote it. The Gradual sings the refuge and eternity clauses without that heading. Psalm 118
does not give these selected verses an independently fixed occasion. Haydock generally attributes Psalm 118
to David, while reporting three conjectures: David writing to instruct the young Solomon, David writing
in his youth under Saul’s persecution, or Daniel consoling the captives. The displayed reign follows the
historical Catholic Encyclopedia’s “usual chronology” of David. Conditional on Davidic attribution, it dates
neither the Psalm’s occasion nor the utterance of verse 81.41
The collection-wide outer boundary comes from the reviewed USCCB Psalms introduction. It does not
establish a common composition date for Psalms 89, 113, and 118, or resolve their individual occasions.
The Alleluia’s Exodus is different again: an event remembered by a later song. The historical “Biblical
Chronology” article gives the Vulgate and Septuagint intervals between Exodus and the beginning of the
Temple, discusses substantial chronological difficulties, and proposes its own reconstruction. The table
preserves the two transmitted relative intervals used in the reviewed chronology, with their actual endpoint.
It does not convert either into an absolute Exodus year or claim that the Psalm was composed when the
Temple was begun.42

Matthew: the location of the discourse and competing composition dates
Matthew 17:21 places Jesus and the disciples in Galilee; 17:23 names Capharnaum. Chapter 18 begins “At
that hour,” and 19:1 narrates the subsequent departure from Galilee toward Judea beyond Jordan. These
boundaries locate the discourse in the Gospel’s narrative movement. They do not identify a particular room
for the parable or assign it a day or year. The parable itself depicts a king and servants without supplying
their geographical coordinates.
The historical “St. Matthew” article reports several competing composition estimates, including traditions
about the apostles’ departure from Palestine and an uncertain interpretation of Irenaeus. It discusses
whether the first written form was Hebrew or Aramaic and how that relates to the extant Greek Gospel.
The Matthew article also reports the early estimate favored by many Catholic critics of its period; “New
Testament” supplies the estimate around the middle of the first century. The table deliberately retains the
distinct estimates rather than averaging them or treating the earliest as the date of the extant Greek form.
They are bounded historical proposals represented in the reviewed corpus, not a claimed present consensus.
Their disagreement has no power to relocate the parable within Matthew’s own sequence.43

Twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost                                                     Appendix: Scope and Qualifications

Ephesians: an imprisoned writer and the readers of the letter
Ephesians 6:20 describes the speaker as an ambassador in a chain. The historical “Epistle to the Ephesians”
article reasons within Pauline authorship and captivity, distinguishing possible imprisonment at Caesarea
from the greater freedom of action associated with Rome. Its broader interval and the more precise year
in “St. Paul” are different historical estimates, not two episodes of composition. The recipient question is
also distinct from the writing-place question: Ephesus and neighboring communities or a wider circular
readership in Asia Minor are alternatives discussed by the article. The passage does not say that the armor
exhortation was spoken on a battlefield at Ephesus. Its martial images address Christian endurance and
prayer.44


Appendix: Scope and Qualifications
This study concerns the Twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost in the 1962 Roman Missal on 18 October
2026 under the general calendar. No diocesan, religious, or titular calendar has been supplied. The mission
addition and St Luke commemoration have the conditions stated in the opening; neither imports another
Mass’s readings or Preface. The two readings are editorial constructions from compatible arguments in the
cited witnesses. Their authors did not all preach on this complete formulary.
The principal early witnesses are Chrysostom, Augustine, and Gregory. Aquinas supplies a later theological
distinction; Bellarmine supplies later Catholic Psalm exposition; Schuster offers a modern historical liturgical
reading. Their differences of purpose and period remain visible. Chrysostom’s disputed explanations of
Ephesians are identified against his historical English editor’s notes. Augustine’s and Chrysostom’s strong
warnings about forfeited pardon are not erased by Aquinas’s more precise distinction. Augustine’s future
judgment and Schuster’s present deprivation of truth are related interpretations, not identical glosses.
Contextual ancient social examples and polemic are not silently promoted into pastoral prescriptions.
The study depends on the acquired historical editions and retained transcriptions listed below. It does
not offer a fresh critical Greek or Latin edition. The lawful Missal transcription and historical English are
taken from the reviewed text collation; normalized typography is not a new translation. Modern source
introductions and the current Missal scan are evidentiary sources with their own rights, not a license to
reproduce their complete publications. Exact machine-readable source bindings and evidence limits remain
in the canonical research dossier.
The work’s substantive boundaries are deliberate: no new local calendar decision, textual conjecture, or
claim of exhaustive scholarly consensus is supplied. The study asks how these appointed words can be read
coherently in the company of identifiable Christian interpreters, while leaving their actual reasoning and
disagreements available to the reader.
